To evaluate the reduction of the posted speed limit to 25 mph, Lee Engineering will complete a level of service
and capacity analysis for the corridor. Base traffic volumes will be established through 27 turning movement
counts at all the signalized intersections on Lead and Coal Avenues from Broadway Boulevard to Washington
Street. Intersection performance metrics will be reported using Synchro for the existing 30 mph speed limit
and a 25 mph speed limit scenario.
Lee Engineering will complete a best practices and literary search regarding posted speed limit reductions
and agency experience. The focus of the research will be on before and after speed compliance and crash
effects.
Along with the speed limit reduction options, Lee Engineering will explore alternative speed reduction
treatments, including but not limited to gateway treatments, wide striping, narrowing lanes, landscaping,
and strategic retro-reflectivity.
Additionally, Lee Engineering will investigate reports of drivers turning from the wrong lane and explore
potential mitigation treatments. Lee Engineering will project crash impacts based on any available crash
modification factors and engineering judgment.
Recommendations will be accompanied by a preliminary implementation plan and cost estimates for the
implementation.
INITIATIVE 2.  REDUCTION TO SINGLE-LANE
Lee Engineering will evaluate the feasibility of reducing the number of lanes on Lead and Coal Avenues to 1
in each direction.
Lee Engineering will collect turning movement counts for Lead and Coal Avenues as well as Lomas Boulevard,
Central Avenue, Garfield Avenue, and Gibson Boulevard.
Lee will complete a field visit to confirm the existing intersection and lane geometry and signal phasing.
Traffic diversion will be estimated by balancing travel times and delays amongst the corridors.
Measures of effectiveness (MOE) will be estimated using Synchro traffic software. The reported MOEs will
include vehicle delays and level of service. Included in the analysis will be a left-turn operations analysis.
No analysis will be completed for future scenarios as the project area is near full buildout.
Lee Engineering will project crash impacts based on any available crash modification factors and engineering
judgment.
Recommendations will be accompanied by a preliminary implementation plan and cost estimates for the
implementation.


=== PDF PAGE 113 ===

Page 3 of 4

INITIATIVE 3.  CONVERT TO TWO-WAY OPERATIONS
Lee Engineering will evaluate the feasibility of changing the corridor to two-way operations on both Lead and
Coal Avenues. The analysis will also estimate the traffic diversion and impacts on other corridors. Lee will
complete a field visit to confirm the existing intersection and lane geometry and signal phasing.
Lee Engineering will collect turning movement counts for Lead and Coal Avenues as well as Lomas Boulevard,
Central Avenue, Garfield Avenue, and Gibson Boulevard. Traffic diversion will be estimated by balancing
travel times and delays amongst the corridors. Measures of effectiveness reported will include vehicle delays
and level of service. Traffic diversion will be estimated by balancing travel times and delays amongst the
corridors.
Measures of effectiveness (MOE) will be estimated using Synchro traffic software. The reported MOEs will
include vehicle delays and level of service. Included in the analysis will be a left-turn operations analysis. No
analysis will be completed for future scenarios as the project area is near full buildout.
Lee Engineering will project crash impacts based on any available crash modification factors and engineering
judgment. Recommendations will be accompanied by a preliminary implementation plan and cost estimates
for the implementation.
INITIATIVE 4.  NOISE ASSESSMENT
Lee Engineering will complete up to ten noise level measurements throughout the corridor. Each of these
measurements will be compared to the FHWA Guidance for roadway sound levels and mitigations.
Lee Engineering will document the impacts of persistent noise levels versus nuisance noise levels. Lee
Engineering will document standard noise mitigation techniques and discuss the pros and cons of each.
Lee Engineering’s 2023 roadway volumes, speed, and classification counts will be documented. Specifically,
the truck volumes will be extracted for use and discussion.
Lee Engineering will research and document the City’s noise level ordinances and options for enforcement.
Lee Engineering will research and document options for truck restrictions. Cost estimates will be prepared
for applicable mitigation options.

this Study on your behalf, and I look forward to working with you on this Project.

Paul Barricklow, PE, PTOE

Subject:
Re: Lead and Coal Public Meeting 3 Slides
Attachments:
DOWNTOWN-Walkability+Analysis.pdf
Hi Paul & Team,

Unfortunately, I couldn't make it to the December public meeting, but I just reviewed the slides and have
some comments. Maybe some of them can be addressed in the report.

For the speed studies (slide 15-18) can you also calculate/plot the 85th percentile speed? It
could be an additional horizontal line.

In our working group meeting you had shown Pedestrian LOS (e.g. based on signal timings).
These were not in the final slides. I hope these are presented in the report.

For the Queuing study, it would be good to have an indication of how often the
queuing condition occurs. If it only occurs for one hour, during peak hour, it might be a good
trade-off to accept some queuing for enhanced safety and walkability throughout the day.
Similar for the vehicle LOS (are these based on the worst conditions? how often do those
conditions happen?)

On slide 32, does going to a single lane configuration really increases the travel time from 2.5
minutes to 12.5 minutes? Seems unrealistic to me. At that point I would assume drivers would
look for alternate routes. But also, if this only happens for 10 minutes a day it might be
acceptable.

Thank you for including the pedestrian LTS. The single-lane configuration does the best at
reducing the LTS, but it would still remain mostly at LTS 3. Two comments:
o In the report it would be good to discuss/recommend what would be needed to get the
entire (or most of) study area to LTS 2
o Are you sure LTS was calculated correctly? From the Existing Conditions details on slide
57, the sidewalk width is 8', and the buffer (buffer + bikelane) is 9', which would suggest
LTS of 2. (But also, I don't think the sidewalks are 8'... from my calculations they are closer
to 6.5')

In our working group, you mentioned that with the single lane configuration drivers might misuse
the large buffer. I just want to point out that this has been done successfully in Albuquerque (on
Lead & Coal nonetheless!). On the bridge over the railroad tracks, Lead has a 13' buffer (from a
previous lane reduction I'm guessing). The proposed 10' buffer is feasible.

There are a few things to note for the stretch west of the highway (Huning Highlands, my
neighborhood)

=== PDF PAGE 215 ===
2
o The newly adopted bike plan calls for protected (vertical separation) bike lanes west of the
highways and assigns this a "high priority". This should be incorporated into the proposal.
o While you only showed a single road profile for the entire study area, west of the highway
the road width is 30' (compared to 25' east of the highway). There might be more room to
play here, e.g. to go to two-way traffic with a two-way cycle track.

I appreciate all the work done for the "enhanced safety" option, and think many of those
elements should be used even for the one-lane or two-way configurations. However, I still believe
maintaining two-lane one-way configuration will not be sufficient to truly enhance safety.
o I am attaching the Albuquerque Downtown Walkability Analysis done in 2014 by Jeff Speck.
On page 18 he argues against 2-lane one-ways: "Drivers tend to speed on multiple-lane
one-way streets, because there is less friction from opposing traffic, and due to the
temptation to jockey from lane to lane. In contrast, when two-way traffic makes passing
impossible, the driver is less likely to slip into the “road racer” frame of mind."
o Personally, I would prefer to solve this problem once and for all, even if it means having to
wait to secure some additional funding (e.g. two-way conversion is significantly more
expensive). One option is a two-way conversion west of the highway to continue the
downtown configuration, and the one-lane option east of the highway where the right-of-
way is narrower and would not support two-way bike lanes.

Thanks again for this great work and presentations. I'm looking forward to seeing the report!

Best,
Carlos

--
Carlos A. Michelen Strofer, PhD

Feedback: Followup Questions I/IV
In advance of the January 29 Lead Coal Task Force meeting and your preparation of a draft study report, I
am submitting several questions.

Please respond in email, and, if necessary, in the meeting.

I request, also, that these questions be included in public comments for the study.

Most of these questions have been raised in previous communication.  If you have previously replied,
please refer me to those responses.

In order to help track these questions, I will be submitting them in a series of separate emails.

Follow Up Question I: Road Departure/Off Road Crash Reporting

1. Will you be reporting road departure/off road crash data in your report for the study?
2. If so, what is the basis for any data on Lead-Coal or elsewhere in Albuquerque?  APD and DMD have
previously reported in the LC Working Group that they did not/do not collect this data on accident
reports.
3. Is there, then, reliable road departure/off road crash data (historical or ongoing) for APD/DMD, or
not?

Followup Questions II/IV: Cross Street Driver Behavior
1. Is the study measuring or compiling data on cross street driver behavior?

2. Specifically, is the study measuring or bringing forward previous data on north-south speed across
signal intersections?

3. The intersections with greatest risk of high speed collisions onto sidewalks and into adjacent homes
are the signal intersections (at Stanford, Girard-2, Bryn Mawr, Carlisle-2,Wellesley and Columbia).  What
do we know, in total, about north-south driver behavior as a factor in collisions at these locations (speed,
red light running)?

4. Do your proposals for mitigation include any measures directed at north-south driver behavior?

Subject:
Followup Questions III/IV: Noise Data
1. What, as precisely as possible, was the location of noise meters?  How many feet from the roadway?

2. In large part because of signalization, traffic flow and traffic noise on Lead-Coal (in my area) follow a
relatively tight wave pattern: a pulse of traffic and noise followed by a period of quiet.   If the reported
noise averages capture both active and quiet periods, then the intensity of noise exposure as a platoon
moves past will be under measured.  Can you (or the noise consultant or a third party) go back into the
noise measurements, confirm this phenomenon, and correct for it?

3. Peak vehicle noise is probably greatest at and immediately downstream of signal intersections.  What
was the location of the noise meters vis-a-vis traffic signals?

Subject:
Lead-Coal Washington to Yale: vertical and horizontal curves [Filed 12 Sep 2024 11:51]
Categories:
Filed by Mail Manager
Hi Paul,

I've had the chance to look at the slides from the Lead-Coal meeting last week.

I was encouraged to see that your slide on area characteristics includes (roadway) curves.

The Washington to Yale section is notable for several curves, both horizontal and vertical. Especially in
combination with the narrow ROW and shallow side setbacks, these curves create easily predictable and
identifiable sightline deficits.

I encourage you and your team to evaluate some of these locations including how the approach of two
unidirectional travel lanes affects sightlines.

Horizontal curves

Coal and Harvard: crossing south to north from SE corner
Lead and Montclaire: crossing south to north from SE corner
Lead and Solano: crossing south to north from SE corner

Vertical curves:

Coal and Hermosa: crossing south to north from SE corner
Lead and Amherst: crossing south to north from SE corner.

As I explained in my public comments, the Washington to Yale section has both site-specific (the above
examples) and generalized sightline limitations.  For notable examples of the generalized problem, I
suggest your team look at:

Coal and Cornell: crossing north to south from NW corner

Lead/Coal feedback
Thank you, Ms. Gabaldon and everyone from Lee Engineering, for presenting at the community meeting
on December 18. I enjoyed learning about the various ways data has been collected and the possible
options for improving safety and noise pollution in the Lead/Coal corridor.

At the meeting I asked how we actually decide on the options that we would like and was told to give
feedback. So here is that feedback! :)

First Choice: Enhanced Safety Options - Single Lane (Protected Bike Lane),
Slide 72.

Second Choice: Enhanced Safety Options - Single Lane, Slide 71.

Third Choice: Enhanced Safety Options - Enhanced Safety Options, Slide 69.

Here are the reasons I prefer these options in this order:

I used to live in a place that required a car to go everywhere, and I moved to Columbia and Coal
specifically because I want to walk or ride my bike to my daily activities. And I do actually walk all over my
neighborhood to stores, restaurants, UNM and CNM. I also take the ART and ride my bike. I hardly ever
drive my car. So my preference is to make my neighborhood safe, reducing accidents and noise and air
pollution. As a pedestrian I find it much safer to cross a one-way street, and one lane is easier to cross
than two. It is also safer and quieter when there is less traffic and when that traffic is slower. Twenty-five
mph or slower is ideal. Possible traffic delays are not important to me and I would be happy if we could
reduce vehicle traffic as much as possible and/or spread it more evenly across all our neighborhood
streets because it is currently too concentrated on Lead and Coal. I love the idea of bump-outs to make
north-south streets narrower at the intersections, such that car traffic has to slow down a lot to turn onto
them. Also, I cannot in good conscience allow my teenager to use the bike lines as they are today: they
need to be separated from car traffic, and that car traffic needs to be much slower!

I am very much NOT in favor of two-way traffic on Lead and Coal. It will be expensive and make crossing
streets trickier than it is now.

Thanks again for your time and efforts. Have a great holiday!

Looking forward to a quieter and safer new year,

Rose Pezzuti Dyer

Dear Mr Barricklow:
Lead and Coal Studies Public Meeting Feedback: stay focused
Please accept the following, and the referenced attachment, as public comments of record for
the ongoing Lee Engineering Lead and Coal Studies.
My comments are in response to your November 14, 2024 Lead Coal public meeting.
I encourage you in the remainder of your study and in your study report to stay focused on
where and what the problem is that you have been engaged to work on. The problem is the
dangerous crash conditions alongside our homes on Lead and Coal Avenues from Washington
St to Yale Blvd. Your effort must focus on making this section of the roadway safe for the
families who live, walk, and bike along it.
Please understand that it is the sustained effort of families along this roadway section, in
response to those conditions, that has led to your study.
Our families’ effort was responsible for City of Albuquerque (CABQ) Mayor Tim Keller’s
2018-2019 Lead Coal Task Force. During that process we recommended (and received broad
support - including from NMDOT- for) a Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) Road Safety
Audit (RSA) on Lead Coal from Washington to Yale. In October of 2019, after initial opposition,
Department of Municipal Development (DMD) Director Pat Montoya ordered the FHWA to
conduct the RSA we had recommended. Despite having been promised by the Mayor himself,
the RSA was killed 2 months later, before it had even started, with never an explanation.
It was our continuing effort that then led to the June 2022 FHWA Lead Coal RSA. (As a
“pedestrian-focused” study, it appears to have been structured deliberately to deny and avoid a
look at road safety conditions along the corridor.)
And it was our families that called, successfully, for the creation of the (fall 2022-November
2024) Mayoral Lead Coal Working Group, whose purpose was to implement recommendations
of the RSA. As you of course know, it was the Working Group process that resulted in your Lead
and Coal Studies, charged to evaluate several of those recommendations.
1

=== PDF PAGE 237 ===
Finally, please be aware that it was our families that asked our state legislators to support our
effort on Lead-Coal and that it is their capital outlay dollars which now fund your study. That
funding was always for and about the dangerous conditions on our section of Lead-Coal.
There are two problems with Lead-Coal from Washington to Yale. The immediate problem is the
road itself. DMD is operating a principal arterial on narrow residential side streets. I’ve
previously pointed out to you in detail the many obvious road safety conditions, both generalized
and location specific. This should need no explanation. Of course the road is dangerous. Of
course it’s substandard.
The second problem is the operation of the roadway. DMD, and a series of Mayoral
administrations including the current, have, over decades, been indifferent to how harmful it is to
operate a principal arterial on only 60 feet of right of way, with traffic just 15 feet away from our
homes.
So while our families see block after block of explosive crashes onto our sidewalks and into our
homes; while we see rollover crashes into our front, back and side yards; while we see ejection
fatality and pedestrian crash victims in front of our living room windows and brain matter on our
streets and in our yards, what has DMD said, forever? “Nothing to see here.Your crash rates
are fine.”
A heads up, then, to you, Albuquerque Vision Zero, DMD, the Mayor, and the Mid Region
Metropolitan Planning Organization (MR-MPO): if the crash conditions on a street make the
people who live along it justifiably afraid to exist in their homes or stand in their yards or walk on
their sidewalks, something is deeply wrong. If you can’t see that this is wrong because your
crash statistics say there’s no problem, well, clearly the problem is your use of statistics.
So, Lead Coal is not, then, just another generic traffic calming problem. Consequently, as I’ve
said before, it's unclear whether your conventional analysis and methodologies are relevant
here. You need to focus not on where else cars might go if CABQ does what’s needed to protect
us, you need to put a stop to where the cars are going now: across bike lanes, onto sidewalks,
and into our homes.
In addition to staying focused on what and where the problem is, I encourage you to be
cognizant of your obvious built in bias here and to avoid unconsidered endorsement of what
DMD is doing. Because what our DMD has been doing on Lead from Washington to Yale –for
decades– is beyond harmful. More of the same is not ok. Your job is not to “make it work.” Your
job is to make us safe.
Instead of more of the same, it’s time for thoughtful consideration of just what is reasonable to
expect of our streets. It’s time for the Mayor and DMD to get real. They need to create a safe
traffic plan for the narrow, residential side streets they have, not the high speed high volume
2

=== PDF PAGE 238 ===
roadway they wish they had and that DMD failed to build when they spent $32M to fix Lead
Coal.
Also, I encourage you to avoid any appearance that your intention is to obfuscate what has
happened on Lead-Coal. CABQ’s actions on Lead-Coal, over decades, do, indeed, give the
appearance of obfuscation and cover up even. You don’t want to be perceived as enabling any
such effort.
In that regard I’m providing as an attachment to this letter the 2010 NEPA document for the
Lead and Coal Avenues Improvements Project (LCIP). The officially documented purpose of
LCIP was to fix the crash problem that we are still dealing with. That’s not what DMD told the
USDOT and until explained otherwise, it appears this is how DMD evaded a road safety study
for the project.
So, stay focused on what and where the problem is. And remember that even though DMD
may be cutting the check for the Lead and Coal Studies, and for your next on-call project for
them, your duty is to the public and specifically to the families who have made your study
possible and who have made very clear what your study needs to be about.
Below is an image of the most recent high impact crash onto the sidewalk at the NE corner of
Coal and Cornell. Be sure in your images for this project to include photos that exemplify the
countless crash scenes like this outside our homes. You don’t want to give the appearance of
minimizing our problem.
Sincerely
Joseph Aguirre

January 27, 2025



Paul Barricklow PE

Tim Brown
Traffic Engineering Division Manager

RE Lead and Coal Studies: Road Safety and Standard of Care

As you head towards concluding the Lead and Coal Studies, I recommend that you make clear
-and make clear in your final report- what the scope of work is regarding any examination of the
safety of the Lead-Coal roadway (ie “road safety”). I also recommend that you make clear to the
community what any relevant engineering standard of care may be regarding the need for a
road safety study in this matter.

As I understand the scope of the Lead and Coal Studies, it does not look at whether the
Lead-Coal roadway is safe: not in its entirety, not for any section, and not for any site-specific
location.The study is blind to the question. It appears to assume, without stating such, that the
roadway itself is safe.

If this is the case, then, I recommend you not represent in the study report that you have looked
at the safety of the roadway. Your look at “comparable” roadways or your singling out of any
specific feature of Lead-Coal between Washington St and Yale Blvd and citing that the same
feature is found in other settings (for example that “homes on Indian School are also 15 feet
away from the roadway”) does not constitute a road safety study.

If the current study does not itself look at the safety of the Lead-Coal roadway, I encourage you
to refer to any previous examination of road safety, including -and specifically-  for the section
from Washington to Yale. In my 20 year experience as a citizen advocate for Lead-Coal no such
study has ever been done.

Moreover, not only has a road study never been done, the City of Albuquerque (CABQ) and the
Department of Municipal Development (DMD) have repeatedly evaded a road safety study of
Lead-Coal: in the $32M federally funded Lead and Coal Avenues Improvements Project (safety
document 2010); in the $120M federally funded Albuquerque Rapid Transit Project (safety
document 2015); in Mayor Keller’s December 2019 cancellation of an already requested FHWA
1

=== PDF PAGE 244 ===
Road Safety Audit (RSA) on Lead-Coal from Washington to Yale; and in the 2022 FHWA RSA
which, as a “pedestrian” audit, precluded any look at conditions of the roadway.

It is demonstrably unsafe to operate a high volume, high speed roadway -to operate two lanes
of busy traffic whether unidirectional or bidirectional- on our narrow residential side streets. If it
is safe –if there’s nothing to hide– why has CABQ repeatedly evaded a full, unbiased look at
road safety as a factor in the crash problem on our roadway section?

If the current study is not looking at road safety and there is no previous road safety study to
refer to, you are then necessarily constrained in the scope of your final report. Your analysis
must focus on and clearly state to what extent any mitigation measure will do what the FHWA to
its credit made clear in its 2022 report is the purpose of this exercise: make Lead and Coal
Avenues safe for the people who live, walk and bike alongside them. Or, to express that
purpose in the vernacular: keep the damn cars on the road.

1. Absent a road safety study, you have no basis to conclude that for the roadway from
Washington to Yale (the section of intense community concern since January 2018) the current
traffic configuration –or even its tweaked, “enhanced safety” version– is safe. Again, it is
demonstrably not.

2. Absent a road safety study, you have no basis to conclude that the bidirectional option would
be safe, or safer than the current configuration. A priori, the significant sightline obstruction
present all along the Washington to Yale section would be as bad or worse in a bidirectional
configuration.

3. You do have a basis to conclude that the single lane option would, by many factors, best
protect the safety of residents, pedestrians and bicyclists 24/7/365 along the Washington to Yale
section.

4. Absent a road safety study, you have no basis to refute or dismiss the FHWA’s conclusion
that a 25 mph speed limit -of course, strictly managed- is indicated to keep the cars on the road.
And, you have no basis to refute the sustained, and well substantiated community
recommendation for a 25 mph speed limit in the Washington to Yale section.

So, please, clarify your scope and adhere to it. You may reasonably acknowledge the absence
of a road safety study. I strongly suggest you do so in your report.  You may not imply that the
roadway is safe and that the demolition derby outside our homes is just on the drivers.  And, the
conclusions in your report must be laser focused on what measures will work best to keep
residents, pedestrians, and cyclists safe.

Finally,  Lee Engineering (in this study) and DMD (in its decades long management of crash
safety on Lead-Coal) give the appearance of treating a critical crash safety problem without an
adequate diagnostic examination. What is the relevant engineering standard of care here?
When is a “road safety” study indicated?
2

=== PDF PAGE 245 ===
We all look forward to putting the Lead-Coal matter to rest, finally. Beyond a definitive safety
solution, that will necessitate learning why it has taken CABQ decades to fix the problem. If a
road safety study should have been done decades ago, the community deserves to know that.

Thank you for your work.

Sincerely,

Joseph Aguirre
Spokesperson, Lead Coal Safety Brigade

Cc: Jennifer Turner, JD: Director, DMD; Lisa Keefe, City Attorney; City Councilor Nichole
Rogers; State Senator Antoinette Sedillo Lopez; State Representative Marianna Anaya;
Community Members; Mayor Keller ℅ Doug Small Director, Public Affairs

Photo: Coal Ave and Cornell Dr, notorious for high impact road departure crashes putting
pedestrians and residents at risk of injury and death. Obvious significant impairment of the
sightline of traffic approaching on Coal for drivers crossing on Cornell. Don’t put this dangerous
intersection on the drivers: that sounds like a cover up.
